READING

**The grant threshold: does PENDLARROW actually reach 30%?**

The 31.8 per cent figure given in the brief is calculated on the year-to-March-2026 turnover base. The grant is not assessed then. It is assessed on 2027-04-30 and reads the annualised value of the work in force on that date. By that date, small animal will have grown another year at eleven per cent.

Small animal 2025-26: £1,840,000 − £504,000 = £1,336,000.
One further year at 11 per cent: £1,336,000 × 1.11 = £1,482,960, call it £1,483,000.
Farm and equine in force at assessment: £504,000 existing + £118,000 Ardgowrie = £622,000.
Total in force: £622,000 + £1,483,000 = £2,105,000.
Farm and equine share: £622,000 ÷ £2,105,000 = **29.5 per cent**.

That is below the thirty per cent floor. The threshold requires farm and equine to be at least £631,500 of a £2,105,000 base. The gap is roughly £9,500 of additional contracted farm or equine work that is not currently in prospect—farm and equine has been flat for three years before Ardgowrie. The gap is small enough that some residual growth in existing farm clients could in theory close it, but on current trajectory it will not.

The consequence is serious: if the thirty per cent threshold is not met on 2027-04-30, the grant is not paid. PENDLARROW's entire financial architecture rests on that £100,000. Without it:

- The practice has spent £260,000 on the fit-out plus £34,000 on the vehicle = £294,000 out, leaving £16,000 from deposit, an extremely thin operating buffer for a practice opening a new surgery and absorbing a new vet.
- The herd health commitment to April 2030 still stands, including the full repayment clause if the practice ever drops below 700 cattle.
- The Ardgowrie contract has a net annual contribution of roughly £47,000 if the vehicle is treated as capital (depreciated over five years: £6,800 p.a.) or only £13,000 if the £34,000 is an annual lease cost. Neither sum is commensurate with the obligations accepted.

Even on the optimistic reading where the grant is paid:

- Cash out: fit-out £260,000 + vehicle £34,000 = £294,000. Remaining: £16,000.
- Grant in (after assessment, against dated invoices, so months later): £100,000.
- Net cash restored to £116,000.

That is less comfortable than WESTERGATE's immediate £50,000 position, and it arrives only after the assessment risk is resolved.

**The night call-out signal**

The outgoing practice held Ardgowrie for nine years—a length of tenure that suggests genuine commitment—and gave it up. Their stated reason on the handover call was the night call-out load. That is explicit and specific. Dairy herds of 900 cows generate a continuous calving, mastitis and metabolic emergency workload. For a practice whose income is 72.6 per cent small animal—and whose next investment (Ordsall Green) is entirely small animal—building and sustaining a night rota for a large dairy farm is a structural misfit. Kirstie Ballantyne-Rowe moving with the contract reduces handover risk and is genuinely useful, but she cannot absorb the full night burden alone. The practice would need to staff a rota, and that rota does not go away until April 2030 at the earliest.

**The lock-in tail**

If the grant is paid and then Ardgowrie later terminates or moves the contract before April 2030, the practice must hold an alternative herd health contract of 700 or more cattle to avoid full repayment of the £100,000. Finding a 700-cattle replacement quickly, in a market where farm and equine has been flat for three years, is not reliable. The grant becomes a contingent liability sitting over the business for 3.5 years.

**WESTERGATE's position**

WESTERGATE is not cost-free: forgoing £100,000 of grant is real money, and the next vet hire goes into small animal at the cost of that hire. But:

- The fit-out is funded directly. £310,000 − £260,000 = £50,000 remaining. No vehicle purchase, no farm vet salary added, no rota to build.
- Farm and equine stays where it stands, the ratio follows its own trajectory without intervention, and there is no contractual obligation to maintain it.
- The practice's growth engine—small animal at eleven per cent for four years—receives the next hire and the benefit of the new surgery, not a flat farm business.
- No contingent repayment liability exists.

**Head-to-head summary**

| | PENDLARROW | WESTERGATE |
|---|---|---|
| Grant achievable at assessment | Probably not (~29.5%) | N/A |
| Immediate cash position | £16,000 (before grant) | £50,000 |
| Annual Ardgowrie net contribution | £13,000–£47,000 | nil |
| Night rota obligation | Yes, to 2030 | No |
| Contingent grant repayment | £100,000 if contract lost | nil |
| Strategic fit | Against growth trajectory | Aligned |

PENDLARROW's case depends entirely on the grant. The grant depends on a ratio that in all probability will not be reached. Without the grant, PENDLARROW adds a thin-margin, high-obligation farm contract to a practice whose staff, capital, and strategic direction are all pointed toward small animal growth.

---

READING
The 31.8 per cent farm-and-equine share cited for PENDLARROW is calculated on the year-to-March-2026 base. The grant assessment reads the annualised work in force on 2027-04-30, by which date eleven per cent annual small-animal growth lifts the denominator to approximately £2,105,000, giving a farm-and-equine ratio of roughly 29.5 per cent—below the thirty per cent floor. The grant on which the entire course depends therefore in all probability will not be paid. Without it, the practice takes on a night-call-intensive 900-cattle contract that the previous specialist holder surrendered after nine years citing that same load, locks itself into a herd health obligation until April 2030 with a £100,000 repayment clause attached, and is left with approximately £16,000 in reserve after the fit-out and vehicle purchase, all in service of a net annual margin on the Ardgowrie contract that ranges from £13,000 to £47,000 depending on how the vehicle cost is treated. WESTERGATE declines all of that, funds the fit-out directly from deposit, leaves £50,000 in reserve, and directs the next hire into the small-animal business that has grown at eleven per cent for four consecutive years and is the explicit purpose of the Ordsall Green surgery.

CALL
WESTERGATE

GROUNDS
Once eleven-per-cent small-animal growth is applied to the April 2027 assessment denominator, the farm-and-equine share falls to roughly 29.5 per cent, below the thirty per cent grant floor, so PENDLARROW's central financial case almost certainly collapses before its operational risks—principally the night-call burden that ended the outgoing practice's nine-year tenure—are even weighed.
